results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It focuses on predictable environment, strict failure behavior, clean temp-space handling, minimal exported environment, and using srun for workload launch.

Example safe_sbatch.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=%x.%j.out        # jobname.jobid.out
#SBATCH --error=%x.%j.err         # separate stderr (optional)
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1              # remove if not using GPUs
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.edu
#SBATCH --export=NONE             # don't inherit the whole environment
#SBATCH --chdir=/home/$USER/work  # or use $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR

# -------------------------
# strict shell safety
set -euo pipefail
umask 0022
IFS=$'\n\t'

# minimal, explicit env exports
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${OMP_NUM_THREADS:-4}
export MY_VAR="value"             # only export what you need

# setup & module environment
module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/12.1   # adapt to your site

# make a per-job temp dir and ensure cleanup
export JOB_TMPDIR="${TMPDIR:-/scratch}/${USER}/job-${SLURM_JOB_ID}"
mkdir -p "$JOB_TMPDIR"
trap 'rc=$?; echo "Job exiting with $rc"; rm -rf "$JOB_TMPDIR"; exit $rc' EXIT

# record runtime info (helps with debugging)
echo "Job: $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME) on $(hostname)"
echo "Started: $(date)"
echo "CWD: $(pwd)"
scontrol show job "$SLURM_JOB_ID" | sed -n 's/^\s*//p' || true

# run your workload with srun (not backgrounded)
# use srun so Slurm tracks processes and signals correctly
srun --mpi=none my_program --threads $OMP_NUM_THREADS --output "$JOB_TMPDIR/out.log"

# explicit success message
echo "Finished: $(date)"

Why these choices
- #SBATCH --export=NONE: avoids leaking local shell environment; explicitly export only needed vars.
- set -euo pipefail + IFS: fails early on errors, undefined vars, and pipeline failures.
- trap/cleanup: ensures temp files are removed and exit code is propagated.
- srun: ensures Slurm tracks tasks and forwards signals; do not background the main work.
- --chdir or cd: avoid relying on caller cwd; scripts run where Slurm expects.
- module purge/load: start from a known module state to avoid hidden dependencies.
- explicit resource directives: helps scheduler and avoids surprise overconsumption.

Extra tips
- Put all #SBATCH directives before any non-comment, non-whitespace line (Slurm ignores later ones).
- Test interactively with salloc/srun before submitting large jobs.
- Avoid running long-lived background processes that outlive the job allocation.
- If you use conda/venv activation, prefer "source /path/to/env/bin/activate" after module load and inside the script (not before sbatch).
- For MPI jobs, use srun --mpi=pmix (or your site's recommended launcher) rather than mpirun unless instructed.

If you want, I can:
- tailor this for multi-node MPI, GPU training, or array-jobs,
- add logging/monitoring hooks, or
- produce a checklist for pre-submit validation. Which would you like?

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a clear, well‑written batch script makes jobs reliable, debuggable, and polite to the cluster. High‑level checklist first, then concrete examples and tips.

Essential structure and rules
- Start with a shell shebang (#!/bin/bash or /bin/sh).
- Put all #SBATCH directives before any non-comment, non-whitespace line; Slurm stops parsing #SBATCH after the first code line.
- Use explicit resource requests (time, nodes, tasks, cpus, memory, gres) so the scheduler can place your job correctly.
- Set safe shell options: e.g., set -euo pipefail (or at least set -e) so failures stop the job.
- Load software (modules/conda) and export runtime env vars in the script — do not assume an interactive environment.
- Use srun for launching parallel or MPI tasks (srun integrates best with Slurm).
- Capture useful output and logs: --output and --error with %j (jobid) or %x (jobname).
- Test with a short run (small time & resources) before scaling up.

Common #SBATCH directives (examples)
- --job-name=NAME
- --output=slurm-%j.out and/or --error=slurm-%j.err
- --time=HH:MM:SS (or D-HH:MM:SS)
- --partition=partition_name
- --account=accountname (if your site uses accounting)
- --nodes=N
- --ntasks=TOTAL_TASKS (or --ntasks-per-node)
- --cpus-per-task=CPUS (for threads/OpenMP / per-process cores)
- --mem=4G or --mem-per-cpu=2G
- --gres=gpu:1 (or gpu:V100:2)
- --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@example.com
- --array=1-100%10 (job arrays, with concurrency limit)

Useful environment variables provided by Slurm
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NAME, SLURM_NODELIST, SLURM_NNODES, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE

Example: single-node multi-threaded (OpenMP)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=omp_test
#SBATCH --output=omp-%j.out
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=16G

set -euo pipefail
module load gcc/12 openmpi
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR

# run the program; use srun for better task placement
srun ./my_openmp_program

Example: MPI, multi-node
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=mpi_job
#SBATCH --output=mpi-%j.out
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=mpi
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=16
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=0

set -e
module load gcc/12 openmpi
cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR

# use srun to launch MPI tasks
srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_program

Example: GPU job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu_train
#SBATCH --output=gpu-%j.out
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:rtx8000:2
#SBATCH --mem=64G

set -euo pipefail
module load cuda/12 cudnn
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR

srun python train.py --batch-size 64

Example: job array (parameter sweep)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=array_ex
#SBATCH --output=array-%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G

PARAM_FILE=params.txt
PARAM=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" $PARAM_FILE)
srun ./run_with_param --param "$PARAM"

Best practices and tips
- Request only what you need. Over‑requesting wastes cluster capacity; under‑requesting causes kills/timeouts.
- Time: set realistic limits. If unsure, overestimate for final runs but test with short limits first.
- Memory: prefer --mem-per-cpu if memory scales with cores; use --mem for per-node memory needs.
- GPUs: use --gres=gpu:<type>:N. Treat GPUs as exclusive resources unless your site supports multi‑tenant GPU sharing.
- CPU binding: for hybrid MPI+OpenMP, set --cpus-per-task and export OMP_NUM_THREADS and consider --cpu-bind=cores.
- I/O: avoid heavy I/O at job start on shared filesystems (stage data to local SSD if available). Write logs incrementally, not just at job end.
- Logs: include meaningful logging to STDOUT/STDERR; use --output and --error to keep per-job logs.
- Reproducibility: record module versions, git commit hashes, conda environment (conda env export), or container image used.
- Fail fast: set -e (or more strict set -euo pipefail) so script exits on errors rather than continuing silently.
- Checkpointing: if long jobs, implement checkpoints or use libraries that can restart.
- Cleanup: remove or compress large temporary files before job end to avoid filling /tmp or shared filesystem.
- Use job dependencies (--dependency=afterok:<jobid>) for multi-step workflows.
- Use srun, not backgrounding processes: Slurm tracks tasks launched with srun properly. If you background things, they may be killed when the script exits.
- Use job arrays for many similar short tasks rather than thousands of single submissions.

Debugging
- Inspect slurm-%j.out and slurm-%j.err.
- Use squeue -j <jobid> and scontrol show job <jobid> for pending reasons.
- For resource usage after completion, use sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,ExitCode.
- If job is pending, squeue (PENDING reason) or scontrol show job gives the scheduler reason.

Politeness to other users / the scheduler
- Don’t hog whole nodes unless needed; use shared packing when safe.
- Use QoS/partition/account correctly.
- Limit job array concurrency with %N in --array to avoid queue flooding.
- Bundle small tasks into arrays or pipelines.

If you want, I can:
- Review one of your scripts and suggest improvements (paste it here).
- Generate a template tailored to your workload (MPI, GPU, OpenMP, Python, containerized).

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Short answer: create a shell script with SBATCH directives and run sbatch <script>. Below are the key steps, a practical example, and common options.

1) Create a batch script (example myjob.sh)
- Start with a shebang and SBATCH header lines (these set job name, partition, resources, time, output file, etc.).
- Load modules and run your commands with srun (or the command directly if single-process).

Example (GPU, 1 node, 4 CPUs, 32GB, 2 hours):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out

module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/12.1
srun python train.py --epochs 10

2) Submit
- sbatch myjob.sh
- You’ll get a job ID printed. Check status with squeue -u youruser or squeue -j <jobid>.
- Cancel with scancel <jobid>.

Useful sbatch command-line options (alternate to #SBATCH lines)
- sbatch -p gpu -J myjob --gres=gpu:1 -t 02:00:00 myjob.sh

Common additional features
- Array jobs: use #SBATCH --array=0-9 and $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in the script.
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> next_job.sh
- Interactive allocation: salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00; then srun --pty bash
- Check partitions/nodes before submitting: sinfo
- Inspect finished jobs: sacct -j <jobid>
- Important env variables: $SLURM_JOB_ID, $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, $SLURM_NTASKS, $SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE, $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

Tips
- Match resource requests to your program (CPUs-per-task for multithreaded code, ntasks for MPI).
- Don’t over-request GPUs or memory; check partition limits (sinfo and local docs).
- Put long-running logs to a file with --output and --error (or a combined --output).

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference and starting point. Tell me if you want deeper examples (MPI, CUDA, Singularity/containers, advanced scheduling) or cluster-specific examples tuned to your environment.

1) What Slurm is (very short)
- Slurm is a cluster workload manager: you request resources, submit jobs, and Slurm schedules them on nodes. Main user commands: sbatch (batch submit), srun (run tasks / job-steps), salloc (interactive allocation), squeue (view queue), scancel (cancel jobs).

2) Typical workflow
- Write a job script with SBATCH directives.
- Submit with sbatch and get a job ID.
- Monitor with squeue and scontrol/sacct.
- Inspect output files (by default slurm-<jobid>.out or use --output).
- Cancel with scancel <jobid> if needed.

3) Minimal batch script example
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --nodes=2
#SBATCH --ntasks=32
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py

Notes:
- sbatch reads lines beginning with #SBATCH before the first non-comment line.
- sbatch returns immediately with the job ID; it does not wait for the job to run/finish.

4) Important SBATCH options explained
- --partition=NAME : which partition/queue to use.
- --nodes=N : number of nodes.
- --ntasks=N : total tasks/ranks (for MPI or task-parallel jobs).
- --cpus-per-task=N : threads per task (for OpenMP, multithreaded).
- --mem or --mem-per-cpu : memory request.
- --gres=gpu:COUNT : GPU resources (example: --gres=gpu:1).
- --time=HH:MM:SS : walltime limit.
- --output=FILE and --error=FILE : stdout/stderr files (use %j for jobid).
- --job-name=NAME : human-readable name.
- --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL : email notifications.

5) srun vs sbatch vs salloc (short)
- sbatch: submit batch script (non-interactive).
- srun: run a task/job-step. Inside a batch script you typically use srun to launch parallel tasks so Slurm tracks them.
- salloc: get an interactive allocation; after salloc you can run srun --pty bash (or srun ... ) to run interactively.

Interactive example:
salloc --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
srun --pty bash

6) Job arrays
- Use arrays for many similar tasks: sbatch --array=1-100%10 job.sh
- Inside the script, use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index inputs.
- %10 limits concurrency to 10 at a time.

7) Dependencies (chaining jobs)
- sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 jobB.sh  (run jobB only if job 12345 finished OK)
- Other types: afterany, aftercorr, singleton, expand:afterok:1234:5678

8) Monitoring and diagnostics
- squeue -u $USER  (view your queue)
- squeue -j <jobid> or scontrol show job <jobid> (detailed)
- sacct -j <jobid> (history/accounting for finished jobs)
- sinfo (partition/node state)
- scontrol show node <nodename> (node details)
- sstat -j <jobid> (live stats for running jobs)
How to find a pending reason: squeue often shows a REASON column; for more detail use scontrol show job <jobid>.

9) Common pending reasons
- Resources (e.g., not enough nodes/GPUs free)
- Priority / fairshare (others have higher priority)
- Partition down or nodes drained
- Job dependency not satisfied
- QOS or user/account limits
You can see specific reason text in squeue or scontrol output.

10) Output files and environment
- Default output file: slurm-<jobid>.out (unless --output set).
- Useful SLURM environment variables: SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID.
- Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES when assigning GPUs (if cluster configured to do so).

11) GPUs tips
- Request with --gres=gpu:N (and ensure partition permits GPUs).
- For conditional submits that depend on idle GPUs, check sinfo for idle GPU nodes first.
- Ask for only what you need (GPU count, GPU memory if available via gres options).

12) Resource-request best practices
- Request accurate walltime: shorter estimates get scheduled earlier.
- Request accurate CPU/memory/GPU — over-requesting wastes queue priority and cluster resources.
- Use job arrays and smaller tasks when possible.
- Add checkpoints or restart logic for long runs.

13) Common troubleshooting steps
- Job pending: squeue -j <id> to get reason; check sinfo for node availability.
- Job failed quickly: inspect the job output file and use sacct -j <id> for ExitCode and elapsed.
- Node down/drained: sinfo -R or scontrol show node to see reasons.

14) Useful commands quick list
- sbatch job.sh  (submit)
- squeue -u $USER  (view your jobs)
- scontrol show job <id>  (job details)
- sacct -j <id>  (history of job)
- scancel <id>  (cancel)
- sinfo  (node/partition status)
- salloc / srun  (interactive/use of resources)

15) Where to learn more
- Official docs: https://slurm.schedmd.com (sbatch, srun, sacct pages).
- Your cluster’s local docs / helpdesk for cluster-specific queues, partitions, QOS, and module environments.

If you want:
- a ready-to-run example for MPI, TensorFlow/PyTorch GPU training, or Singularity containers,
- a checklist to debug a specific job that’s stuck/pending/failing,
- or a walk-through using your cluster’s partition names and constraints—tell me which and I’ll tailor examples.

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It follows common best-practices: defensive shell flags, an EXIT trap that cleans up, use of SLURM-provided env vars, thread-affinity settings, local temp working directory (SLURM_TMPDIR), safe copying of inputs/outputs, and using srun to launch the workload.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#SBATCH --job-name=example-job
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                # remove or change if not using GPUs
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

# Fail fast and safely
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

# Cleanup function and trap (runs on EXIT, INT, TERM)
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "cleanup: job=$SLURM_JOB_ID rc=$rc"
  # kill any child processes started in background (process group)
  kill -- -$$ 2>/dev/null || true
  # attempt to copy results back (best-effort)
  if [[ -d "${TMPDIR:-}" ]]; then
    mkdir -p "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR/results" || true
    rsync -av --remove-source-files "$TMPDIR"/results/ "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"/results/ || true
  fi
}
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

# Prepare local temp working dir (prefer SLURM_TMPDIR if provided)
TMPDIR="${SLURM_TMPDIR:-/tmp/slurm-${SLURM_JOB_ID:-$$}}"
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"
cd "$TMPDIR"

# Load environment (modules/conda) — keep this explicit and repeatable
module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/12.1   # example; adapt to your cluster

# Set deterministic thread counts from SBATCH settings
export OMP_NUM_THREADS="${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}"
export MKL_NUM_THREADS="${OMP_NUM_THREADS}"
export NUM_THREADS="${OMP_NUM_THREADS}"

# Copy input data to local storage (fast I/O)
rsync -av "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"/data/ "$TMPDIR"/data/

# Print context for debugging
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $(hostname) nodes=$SLURM_JOB_NODELIST ntasks=$SLURM_NTASKS cpus_per_task=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"

# Run the job via srun (use mpirun only if your MPI stack requires it)
# If you need background processes, capture PIDs so cleanup can kill them
srun --cpu_bind=cores my_program --epochs 10

# Ensure results are saved back to the submit directory
mkdir -p "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR/results"
rsync -av "$TMPDIR"/results/ "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"/results/

echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID completed."

Concise rationale and tips
- #SBATCH directives must appear before the first non-comment/non-whitespace line. Slurm only reads directives up to the first non-comment.
- Use set -euo pipefail and IFS to fail fast and avoid silent errors.
- Use trap on EXIT/TERM to ensure partial outputs are preserved and background children are killed.
- Use SLURM_TMPDIR (or create a dedicated /tmp path) for I/O-heavy temporary work; copy inputs in and results out with rsync (more robust than plain cp).
- Set OMP_NUM_THREADS / MKL_NUM_THREADS from SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK so threaded libraries don’t oversubscribe CPUs.
- Use srun to launch tasks when running inside an allocation; it integrates with Slurm for job control and affinity.
- Avoid long-running side-effects on shared filesystems without explicit sync; write to local, then rsync back.
- Keep module/environment actions explicit and script-local (don’t rely on interactive shells).
- Add resource-specific directives (gres=gpu:..., --mem=, --cpus-per-task=) to match actual needs — under-requesting causes failures, over-requesting wastes cluster allocation.
- For debugging, add set -x near the top temporarily to echo commands (remove in production).

If you want, I can produce:
- a GPU-training-specific template (with NCCL/MPI tuning and NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME hints),
- an MPI template using srun --mpi=pmix or mpirun for your environment,
- or a short checklist of what to change for checkpointing/restarts. Which would you like?

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a well-written sbatch script makes jobs easier to run, debug, and re-run. Below are concise guidelines, common directives, best practices, and a few practical templates you can adapt.

What to include (in order)
- Shebang and a safe shell: start with #!/bin/bash and set strict mode e.g. set -euo pipefail.
- SBATCH header directives: job name, output/error paths, time, partition, nodes/CPUs/memory/GPU, array/dependencies, QoS/account, mail options.
- Environment setup: module load or conda/venv activation, export variables, use $TMPDIR for node-local scratch.
- Resource-aware launch: use srun for MPI / parallel tasks; set --cpus-per-task and thread affinity for multi-threaded programs.
- Logging & reproducibility: write stdout/stderr to files including %j (jobid), save environment and git commit/conda list if reproducibility matters.
- Error handling & cleanup: trap signals, handle SIGTERM for graceful checkpointing.
- Small, focused commands: keep the script a thin wrapper around your program invocation; long pipelines belong in separate scripts if complex.

Important SBATCH directives (common)
- --job-name=NAME
- --output=path/%x-%j.out and --error=path/%x-%j.err (or use --output and omit --error)
- --partition=partition_name
- --time=HH:MM:SS (request realistic time)
- --nodes=N (for multi-node MPI) or --ntasks=NTASKS
- --cpus-per-task=M (for multi-threaded tasks / OpenMP)
- --mem=MEM or --mem-per-cpu=MEM (pick one)
- --gres=gpu:count (for GPUs) or --gpus=count (site dependent)
- --array=1-100%10 (job arrays with concurrency limit)
- --dependency=afterok:<jobid> (chain jobs)
- --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@domain
- --exclusive (if you need whole nodes)

Best-practice tips
- Request accurate resources. Over-requesting wastes queue time and scheduling; under-requesting causes kills.
- Use --cpus-per-task with threaded programs and set OMP_NUM_THREADS accordingly.
- Prefer --mem-per-cpu when memory scales with cores; otherwise set --mem for whole-node.
- For GPUs: request only what you use (and ensure drivers/containers can see the allocated devices). Test on an interactive GPU node first.
- Use srun to launch parallel tasks (MPI and many multi-process workflows): srun --mpi=pmix my_mpi_program
- Put large temporary files on node-local $TMPDIR or $SCRATCH, and copy results out at job end.
- Use job arrays for many similar tasks instead of submitting many small jobs.
- Add checkpoints or periodic saves if jobs are long-running or preemptible.
- Add #SBATCH --test-only (or sbatch --test-only) to validate script parsing if supported.
- Keep the script portable: avoid user-specific absolute paths; use project/account variables only if needed.
- Save a copy of the job script alongside job outputs for provenance (cp $0 ${OUTPUT_DIR}/job-${SLURM_JOB_ID}.sh).

Simple examples

Minimal single-task job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=test
#SBATCH --output=logs/test-%j.out
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=2G

set -euo pipefail
module load python/3.10
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID running on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
python my_script.py --input data/input.dat

GPU training job (single node, 4 GPUs)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=train
#SBATCH --output=logs/train-%j.out
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gpus=4
#SBATCH --mem=64G

set -euo pipefail
module load cuda/12.0
module load singularity
echo "GPUs visible:"
nvidia-smi
# set threads appropriately
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
srun python train.py --epochs 50 --batch-size 64

Array job (embarrassingly parallel)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=array-job
#SBATCH --output=logs/array-%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --array=1-100%20
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G

set -euo pipefail
TASK_ID=${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}
python process_chunk.py --chunk-id $TASK_ID

Advanced robustness patterns
- Strict shell safety: set -euo pipefail; use trap '...' EXIT to copy outputs back on failure.
- Graceful termination: trap 'echo "SIGTERM caught"; do checkpoint; exit' TERM
- Checkpoint + requeue: use scontrol requeue or sbatch --requeue settings and save progress frequently.
- Containerization: run under Singularity/Apptainer to encapsulate dependencies:
  singularity exec --nv my.sif python train.py

Common pitfalls
- Forgetting to set --cpus-per-task for multi-threaded programs → slow or OOM.
- Using mpirun instead of srun on some clusters (use srun unless docs say otherwise).
- Assuming CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set — not all sites do; test on an interactive node.
- Requesting GPUs but not loading correct drivers/modules or container flags (--nv).
- Putting huge I/O on the shared home directory; use cluster scratch for heavy I/O.

Debugging & profiling
- Test interactively first: salloc or srun --pty bash
- Use sbatch --test-only for syntax checks (if available)
- Inspect job runtime and efficiency: seff <jobid> or sacct --format=JobID,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,State,MaxRSS
- Use sstat for live job resource usage.

Quick checklist before submitting
- Is --time realistic but not excessive?
- Did I set cpus/memory/gpus correctly?
- Are stdout/stderr paths set and writable?
- Did I load required modules / activate env?
- Is temporary I/O on fast node-local storage?
- Is there a plan for checkpoints and cleanup?

- Review a script you already have and point out improvements (paste it here).

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Here's a concise guide to submitting a job with Slurm.

1) Choose interactive vs batch
- Batch (recommended for reproducible runs): create a shell script and run sbatch myjob.sh.
- Interactive (debugging, short work): salloc or srun to get an allocation, then run commands inside it.

2) Minimal sbatch usage
- Command: sbatch myscript.sh
- Quick one-liner: sbatch --time=01:00:00 --mem=4G --cpus-per-task=1 --job-name=test --output=job.%j.out myscript.sh

3) Typical sbatch script layout
- Put #!/bin/bash at top.
- Add SBATCH directives (either in-file #SBATCH lines or as sbatch CLI flags).
Example:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=train-job
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:4
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x.%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

# load environment
module load cuda/11.8 python/3.11
source venv/bin/activate

# run program
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- Use --gres=gpu:<count> to request GPUs.
- Time format is HH:MM:SS (or D-HH:MM).
- Memory units: M, G (e.g., 64G). You can request mem-per-cpu or mem.
- %x is job name, %j is job id in filenames.
- srun inside the script launches tasks within the allocation; sbatch only schedules the script.

4) Useful sbatch options/features
- Job arrays: sbatch --array=1-100 myarray.sh (use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside).
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> next.sh
- QOS/account: --qos=<name>, --account=<acct>
- Partition: --partition=<name> (check sinfo for available partitions)
- Exclusive node: --exclusive

5) Checking and managing jobs
- squeue -u $USER to see queued/running jobs.
- scontrol show job <jobid> or sstat <jobid> for details (sstat for running jobs).
- sacct -j <jobid> for historical accounting after completion.
- Cancel: scancel <jobid>.

6) Tips / troubleshooting
- Inspect job .out/.err files for logs.
- If job stays PENDING, run squeue -j <jobid> to see pending reason; scontrol show job <jobid> may give more detail.
- Check partition/node availability with sinfo.
- Request only resources you need; oversized requests wait longer.
- Use modules or activate your environment inside the script so compute nodes have correct software.

If you want, I can:
- Review a script you have and suggest fixes, or
- Submit a script for you (I’ll need the script or exact sbatch command — if you want me to submit it, tell me and I’ll transfer to the operator to run sbatch).

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Here's a compact, practical Slurm tutorial covering the common workflows, commands, and examples you’ll use day-to-day.

1) Basic concepts
- sbatch: submit a batch script (non-interactive). Scheduler queues and runs it later.
- srun: run a parallel job step (can be used inside a batch job or interactively).
- salloc: get an interactive allocation (then use srun inside it).
- squeue: view queued/running jobs.
- sinfo: view partitions and node states.
- scancel: cancel jobs.
- scontrol: inspect or change Slurm objects (jobs, nodes, partitions).
- sacct: accounting/history for completed jobs.
- gres: generic resources (e.g., GPUs).

2) Typical workflow (quick)
- Write a batch script (see example below).
- Submit: sbatch myjob.sh
- Check queue: squeue -u $USER   (or squeue -j JOBID)
- If stuck: squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %R" to include the pending REASON; use scontrol show job JOBID for details.
- Cancel: scancel JOBID
- Inspect completed jobs: sacct -j JOBID --format=JobID,JobName%20,State,ExitCode,Elapsed

3) Minimal sbatch script example
#!/bin/sh
#SBATCH --job-name=train-model
#SBATCH --partition=gpu               # partition name (cluster-specific)
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                  # request 1 GPU (syntax may vary by site)
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00               # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out         # %j -> job id
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

module load python/3.10 cuda/12.0
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- Adjust partition, gres, modules per your cluster.
- Use --mem-per-cpu if you want memory scaled per CPU.

4) Interactive runs
- Interactive allocation: salloc --partition=gpu --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
- Then inside allocation: srun --pty bash  (or srun --pty python)
- Or for one-off command: srun --partition=short --time=00:05:00 hostname

5) Job arrays and dependencies
- Array: #SBATCH --array=1-100%10  (100 tasks, at most 10 running simultaneously)
- Dependency example: sbatch --depend=afterok:12345 downstream.sh  (run only if job 12345 completes successfully)

6) Useful squeue / scontrol / sinfo usage
- squeue -u $USER              (your jobs)
- squeue -j JOBID              (specific job)
- squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %D %R"   (custom columns incl. REASON)
- scontrol show job JOBID      (detailed per-job info: reason, alloc nodes, TRES)
- sinfo -s                     (partition summary)
- sinfo -N -l                  (one row per node, detailed)
- sinfo -o "%P %D %C %G"       (custom output; check docs for formats)

7) Inspecting running job resource usage
- sstat -j JOBID               (shows CPU%, memory RSS, I/O for running jobs; works only while running)

8) Accounting and history
- sacct -u alice --format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,ExitCode
- sreport for aggregate usage reports (CPU/GPU hours)

9) Common pending reasons & how to act
- Resources: “Resources” or “ReqNodeNotAvail” — requested nodes/GPUs not free; reduce request or wait.
- QOS/Partition limits: QOSMaxWall or QOSLimit — check with admins or pick different QOS.
- Priority: low priority — consider adjusting QOS or wait.
- NodeDown/PartitionDown — check sinfo; contact admin if nodes are down.

10) Best practices & tips
- Test with small resources/time before scaling up.
- Request only what you need (CPUs, mem, GPUs) to improve scheduling.
- Put expensive/long runs in partitions intended for them.
- Use checkpointing for long jobs.
- Check slurm-%j.out for stdout/stderr unless different paths set.
- Use job names and output filenames with %j (jobid) to avoid collisions.
- If a job is pending with no clear reason, run scontrol show job JOBID and share the output with admins.

11) Environment variables available in jobs (handy inside scripts)
- $SLURM_JOB_ID, $SLURM_NODELIST, $SLURM_NTASKS, $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, etc.

12) Where to get help
- Cluster’s local docs or admin (partitions, valid gres, module names, site QOS limits).
- Slurm manpages (srun(1), sbatch(1), squeue(1), sinfo(1), scontrol(1)) — or I can pull exact references.

If you want, I can:
- Provide a ready-to-run sbatch template customized to the partition/gpu count you plan to use.
- Walk through a live example on your cluster (I can run sinfo/squeue to show current state) — tell me which read you want (e.g., "show gpu partition status"), and I’ll fetch it.

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It follows common best practices: fail-fast bash flags, controlled environment setup, temporary scratch use, clean cleanup on signals/exit, use srun for the workload, and explicit resource/QoS directives.

Script (edit SBATCH headers and module/command lines to match your site & job):

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=example_job            # short name
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out               # %x=job-name %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=compute              # change to your partition
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                     # remove if no GPU needed
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
#SBATCH --export=ALL                     # export environment (or list VAR=val)

set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'
umask 0022

# ---- cleanup / trap ----
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "[$(date --rfc-3339=seconds)] Job $SLURM_JOB_ID ended with exit code $rc"
  # Example: copy results back from scratch (adjust to site policies)
  if [[ -n "${SCRATCH_DIR:-}" && -d "$SCRATCH_DIR" ]]; then
    mkdir -p "${SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR}/results/${SLURM_JOB_ID}"
    rsync -a --remove-source-files "$SCRATCH_DIR"/ "${SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR}/results/${SLURM_JOB_ID}/" || true
    rm -rf "$SCRATCH_DIR"
  fi
  exit $rc
}
trap 'cleanup' EXIT TERM

# ---- job header info ----
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME) on $(hostname)"
echo "Started: $(date)"
echo "Working dir: $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"

# ---- prepare scratch / workdir ----
SCRATCH_DIR="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/${USER}_${SLURM_JOB_ID}"
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH_DIR"
cd "$SCRATCH_DIR"

# ---- tuned runtime env ----
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}
export OMP_PROC_BIND=spread

# load modules or activate virtualenv/container
module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/11.8   # adjust to site modules or comment out
# source /path/to/venv/bin/activate   # or use conda, singularity/apptainer, etc.

# optional: quick health checks
command -v nvidia-smi >/dev/null 2>&1 && nvidia-smi || true
echo "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES:-unset}"

# ---- run work (use srun for proper resource launch) ----
# prefer srun for MPI/parallel jobs; plain programs OK for simple single-task jobs
srun --cpu-bind=cores /path/to/my_program --arg val

# ---- normal exit (cleanup trap will run) ----
exit 0

Concise rationale & best practices
- Use set -euo pipefail + safe IFS to reduce shell surprises.
- Keep SBATCH directives at top; prefer resource requests that match actual needs (cpus-per-task, mem, gres).
- Use %x-%j in output/error for unique, informative logs.
- Create per-job scratch (TMPDIR or /scratch) and run there to avoid I/O in shared $HOME.
- Export OMP_NUM_THREADS from SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK so threaded apps respect allocation.
- Use module/venv/container initialization inside the script (avoid relying on interactive env).
- Use srun to launch the work — it ensures Slurm tracks the tasks correctly (especially for MPI/OpenMP/GPU).
- Trap EXIT/TERM to copy logs/results back and do cleanup; avoid losing outputs on preemption.
- Add lightweight health checks (nvidia-smi) to help debugging GPU issues.
- Keep long-running data transfer out of critical path; stage data in/out via rsync and fail-safe copying.
- Prefer explicit --mail-user and --mail-type or cluster notification tools; many sites disable email so check local policy.

Optional extras
- Add job-array support with SBATCH --array and index-aware scratch directories.
- Record git commit/branch or container image for reproducibility.
- Save environment (pip list, conda env export) to the job output for debugging.
- For heavy IO, tune I/O (striping) per site; consult local storage docs.

If you want, tell me the scheduler defaults at your site (partition names, module stack, scratch path) and I’ll tailor this template to your environment.

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a clear, well‑written sbatch script makes jobs reproducible, debuggable, and efficient. Below is a compact checklist, key tips, and a ready-to-adapt example.

Essential structure
- Start with a shell shebang: #!/bin/bash
- Put all Slurm options as #SBATCH directives near the top (one per line). These are parsed by sbatch before the script runs.
- Change to the submit directory: cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
- Load modules / set up the environment, then run your program with srun (or mpirun if your site requires it).
- Capture logs and exit status.

Common #SBATCH directives (examples and purpose)
- --job-name=NAME           (identifies the job)
- --output=job.%j.out       (stdout; use %j for jobid)
- --error=job.%j.err        (stderr)
- --time=HH:MM:SS           (walltime limit)
- --partition=PART          (partition/queue)
- --account=ACCOUNT         (charge account)
- --nodes=1                 (number of nodes)
- --ntasks=1                (total MPI tasks)
- --ntasks-per-node=N
- --cpus-per-task=THREADS   (cores per task; for OpenMP or multithreaded tasks)
- --mem=8G                  (memory per node or --mem-per-cpu)
- --gres=gpu:1              (GPUs per node)
- --array=1-100%10          (job arrays; %N limits concurrent array jobs)
- --mail-user=you@example.com --mail-type=END,FAIL (email notifications)
- --exclude=nodename or --constraint=... (node selection)

Robustness and environment
- Use set -euo pipefail at the top to fail fast on errors.
- Export OMP_NUM_THREADS from SLURM variables: export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}
- Use module load ... or source environment scripts; record module list for reproducibility: module list 2>&1 | tee modules.txt
- Use $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR as working directory; avoid running from $HOME unless intended.

Running your workload
- Use srun for launching parallel work under Slurm (srun integrates with allocation, accounting, node placement). Example: srun my_executable args
- For MPI, prefer srun over mpirun unless your MPI vendor requires mpirun. If you must use mpirun, verify it respects Slurm allocations.
- For multi-threaded tasks: request --cpus-per-task and set OMP_NUM_THREADS accordingly.
- For hybrid MPI+OpenMP: request both ntasks and cpus-per-task and bind threads properly.

Logging, debug, and reproducibility tips
- Record environment and Slurm variables at job start: env | sort > env.txt and echo SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_NODELIST, etc.
- Save stdout/stderr separately and include job id in filenames.
- Add checkpoints or periodic state dumps if long-running.
- Start with a small test (short time, fewer resources) before scaling up.

Performance / placement tips
- Use --exclusive if your job needs entire node(s).
- Use --ntasks-per-node and --cpus-per-task to control core packing.
- Use --hint=multithread or --cpu-bind options if available at your site for NUMA/CPU affinity.
- For GPU jobs, request gres=gpu:N and ensure your job loads the correct CUDA/driver modules.

Common pitfalls
- Under-requesting time causes premature job termination.
- Not matching cpus-per-task with OMP_NUM_THREADS wastes CPUs or causes oversubscription.
- Running mpirun without srun may bypass Slurm's task placement.
- Placing #SBATCH lines after non-comment code — sbatch stops parsing after the first non-comment/non-whitespace line.

Small example template (adapt resources as needed)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=example_job
#SBATCH --output=example.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=example.%j.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

set -euo pipefail
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"

module purge
module load gcc/11 openmpi cuda/12
module list 2>&1 | tee modules.txt

# Set OpenMP threads to match cpus-per-task
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}

# Record job context
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID started on $(date)"
echo "Nodes: $SLURM_NODELIST" > nodes.txt

# Run (use srun to respect Slurm placement)
srun --mpi=pmix ./my_program --arg value

# Capture exit status
echo "Exit code: $?" > exit_status.txt

When to use job arrays, dependencies, or checkpoints
- Arrays: many many similar tasks that are independent — use --array and index via $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID.
- Dependencies: chain jobs using --dependency=afterok:<jobid> to avoid manual waits.
- Checkpoints: long-running jobs should be able to resume (implement periodic saves).

If you tell me the resources and type of job you need (CPUs, GPUs, memory, MPI vs OpenMP, walltime, partition, array size), I can generate a tuned sbatch script template for you.

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Good question — here’s a concise practical guide to submitting jobs with Slurm.

1) Create a batch script
- Start with a shell header: #!/bin/bash
- Put SBATCH directives near the top (they can also be passed on the sbatch command line).

Example minimal script (save as myjob.sh):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00          # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err

module load python
srun python myscript.py arg1 arg2

Notes on common SBATCH options
- --job-name=NAME : readable name shown in squeue
- --partition=PART : which partition/queue to use
- --nodes=N / --ntasks=M : node/task counts
- --cpus-per-task=K : threads per task (OpenMP, etc.)
- --mem=8G or --mem-per-cpu=2G : memory
- --gres=gpu:1 (or gpu:2) : request GPUs
- --time=DD-HH:MM:SS or HH:MM:SS : walltime limit
- --account=projectname : accounting/project charge
- --qos=name : quality of service
- --output=FILE and --error=FILE : job stdout/stderr
- --mail-user=user@example.com and --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL : email

2) Submit the script
- sbatch myjob.sh
sbatch prints the job ID on success.

3) Submit-time overrides
- You can specify SBATCH options on the command line:
sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=04:00:00 myjob.sh

4) Job arrays
- For embarrassingly parallel repeats: add
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
- Inside the script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index work.

5) Interactive/short tests
- For interactive work or debugging:
srun --pty --partition=debug --time=00:30:00 --cpus-per-task=2 bash
or request an allocation with salloc then srun.

6) Check job status and details
- squeue -u $USER  (view queued/running jobs)
- squeue -j <jobid>  (specific job)
- scontrol show job <jobid>  (detailed info)
- sacct -j <jobid>  (after completion for accounting/exit codes)
- Inspect slurm-%j.out (stdout) and slurm-%j.err (stderr)

7) Common troubleshooting
- Pending reasons: check squeue (REASON column) or scontrol show job <jobid>
- If waiting for GPUs/partitions, check node availability with sinfo
- If job fails quickly, check exit code in sacct and examine output/error files

8) Useful environment variables (inside job)
- $SLURM_JOB_ID, $SLURM_NTASKS, $SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE, $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

If you want, I can:
- Review a script you have (paste it) and suggest SBATCH changes,
- Or submit a script for you. (If you ask me to submit a script file, I’ll hand off to the operator to run sbatch.)

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Great — here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference and starter guide. It covers common commands, example job scripts (CPU and GPU), interactive usage, job arrays, resource requests, debugging tips, and best practices.

Quick glossary (commands you’ll use most)
- sbatch: submit a batch script (non-interactive).
- srun: run a command under Slurm (from shell or inside a job).
- salloc: allocate an interactive job allocation.
- squeue: view current queue (running/pending jobs).
- sinfo: view partitions and node states.
- scontrol show job <id>: detailed job information.
- scancel <jobid>: cancel a job.
- sacct: view historical/accounting info about completed jobs.

Minimal single-job batch script (CPUs)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job-%j.err
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00          # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=4               # total tasks (MPI ranks)
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1        # threads per task
#SBATCH --mem=8G                 # per-node memory or use --mem-per-cpu

module load python
srun python train.py --epochs 5

How to submit / inspect / cancel
- sbatch myscript.sh          # submit; prints job id
- squeue -u $USER             # show your running/pending jobs
- squeue --job <jobid>        # single-job view
- scontrol show job <jobid>   # detailed fields (reasons, TRES, stdout/stderr)
- scancel <jobid>             # cancel job

GPU job example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-train
#SBATCH --output=gpu-%j.out
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1           # request 1 GPU
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G

module load cuda/12.0
srun python train_gpu.py

Job array example (many similar tasks)
#SBATCH --job-name=array-job
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10       # 1..100 tasks, max 10 running simultaneously
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --output=array-%A_%a.out

# inside script:
echo "Array index: $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID"

Key resource directives and what they mean
- --nodes / -N : number of nodes.
- --ntasks / -n : number of tasks (MPI ranks).
- --cpus-per-task : threads per task (OpenMP/threads).
- --mem or --mem-per-cpu : memory.
- --gres=gpu[:count] : GPUs per job.
- --time or -t : time limit.
- --partition or -p : partition/queue to use.
- --constraint : node feature (e.g., highmem, avx512).
- --output / --error : capture stdout/stderr (defaults to slurm-<jobid>.out).

Environment variables set in jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID
- SLURM_JOB_NODELIST
- SLURM_NTASKS
- SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (for arrays)
Use these inside scripts to make behavior conditional on Slurm settings.

Interactive usage
- salloc --time=01:00:00 -n4 --gres=gpu:1  # get an allocation then use srun
- srun --pty bash                          # get interactive shell in allocation
Interactive debugging: use small resources and short time to iterate quickly.

Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R"  # customizable columns
- scontrol show job <jobid>      # see pending reason, nodes, TRES
- sinfo                          # partition/node availability
- sinfo -N or sinfo --Node       # one row per node
- sinfo -R                       # nodes in drain/down and reasons
- sacct -j <jobid>               # historical info, exit codes, elapsed
Pending reasons:
- Look at the REASON column in squeue; if not enough resources, it’ll say e.g., "Resources" or "Priority" or "Dependency".
- For more details on a single pending job, use scontrol show job <jobid>.

Output, exit codes, and accounting
- Files default to slurm-<jobid>.out; use --output to set.
- sacct reports State and ExitCode (useful for investigating TIMEOUT or FAILED).
- TIMEOUT happens when jobs exceed --time.

Best practices
- Request realistic resources and sane time limits — oversized requests make scheduling harder.
- Test locally or with a tiny job before scaling up.
- Use job arrays for parameter sweeps instead of many distinct small submissions.
- Use explicit --output/--error paths so logs are easy to find.
- Use modules or environment management to make jobs reproducible.
- For MPI, prefer srun to launch MPI ranks where possible.
- Check sinfo before submitting to pick a partition with available resources.

When to ask admins / check docs
- If squeue shows nodes DOWN or DRAINed, use sinfo -R to see reasons and consult admins.
- For cluster-wide configuration or scheduler tuning questions, check scontrol show config or ask your HPC admin.

Quick troubleshooting checklist
1. Job pending for long? squeue -> check REASON -> scontrol show job <id>.
2. Job failed quickly? Check output/error and sacct -j <id> for ExitCode.
3. Can't find GPU? sinfo shows partition/node GPU counts; use --gres=gpu:N.
4. Need more memory? Increase --mem or use highmem partition/constraint.

If you want, I can:
- Walk through submitting a specific script you have (paste it) and point out improvements.
- Show a short example for MPI (multi-node) or a recommended cluster-specific template.
- Explain any specific pending reason you’re seeing (if you share the job id).

Which of those would you like next?

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It emphasizes fail-fast shell options, a cleanup trap, resource/request directives, minimal environment assumptions, recording runtime context, and using srun for the actual workload.

Example safe_sbatch.sh
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=safe_example          # job name
#SBATCH --output=%x.%j.out               # %x=jobname %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=%x.%j.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00                  # hh:mm:ss
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                     # if you need GPUs
#SBATCH --account=YOUR_ACCOUNT
#SBATCH --qos=regular

# ---- strict shell / safety ----
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

# move to submit dir (Safer than assuming $PWD)
cd "${SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR:-$PWD}"

# ---- simple logging / environment snapshot ----
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID starting at $(date)"
echo "Running on $(hostname)"
echo "Job name: ${SLURM_JOB_NAME:-(none)}"
echo "Command line: $0 $*"
echo "Environment snapshot:"
env | sort

# ---- resource / runtime limits (optional) ----
# Disable core dumps, raise open files soft limit
ulimit -c 0 || true
ulimit -S -n 65536 || true

# ---- cleanup handler ----
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "Job ${SLURM_JOB_ID:-unknown} exiting with status $rc at $(date)"
  # collect simple diagnostics (non-fatal)
  if command -v nvidia-smi &>/dev/null; then
    echo "nvidia-smi:"
    nvidia-smi || true
  fi
  # kill any leftover child processes started by this script
  pkill -P $$ || true
  # place optional log-collection or artifact upload here
}
trap cleanup EXIT

# ---- module / environment setup ----
module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/11.8         # adapt to your stack
# activate venv/conda if needed
# source /path/to/venv/bin/activate

# ---- sanity checks (optional) ----
# ensure GPU is present when requested
if [[ -n "${SLURM_JOB_GPUS:-}" ]] || [[ -n "${CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES:-}" ]]; then
  command -v nvidia-smi >/dev/null && nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total --format=csv || true
fi

# ---- run work: prefer srun inside batch scripts ----
# use srun so Slurm can control and account the task
srun --cpu-bind=cores python train.py --epochs 10

# End of script — cleanup trap will run on exit

Why these elements matter (short):
- set -euo pipefail + IFS: fail fast and avoid common shell pitfalls.
- trap cleanup EXIT: always run diagnostics/cleanup on normal exit or errors.
- cd to SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR: ensures relative paths are correct when job runs on compute node.
- Use srun inside sbatch: lets Slurm launch/monitor tasks correctly (and handle MPI/remote launches).
- Log environment and node info early: helps post-mortem debugging.
- Ulimits: avoid runaway resource usage; customize to site policy.
- Module load / venv activation: keep environment explicit and repeatable.
- Redirected output via --output/--error or %x.%j: predictable logs per job.

Minimal tips:
- Don’t rely on interactive behavior (no sudo, don’t assume modules are loaded).
- Keep sensitive credentials out of scripts; use secure secrets management.
- For long-running jobs, consider periodic checkpointing and capturing exit codes.
- Test scripts with a short --time and small resources before full-scale runs.

If you want, I can:
- produce a variant for multi-node MPI jobs,
- add checkpoint/restart scaffolding, or
- tailor the header to your cluster’s partitions and module names. Which would you like?

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

#!/bin/bash #SBATCH --nodes=1 --constraint=haswell #BB create_persistent name=alpha capacity=10 access=striped type=scratch #DW persistentdw name=alpha #SBATCH hetjob #SBATCH --nodes=16 --constraint=knl #DW persistentdw name=alpha ...

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the
node is powered down). When the node is powered down, the those features
become available but not active. Any feature not defined by

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

The configuration of nodes (or machines) to be managed by Slurm is
also specified in /etc/slurm.conf .
Changes in node configuration (e.g. adding nodes, changing their
processor count, etc.) require restarting or reconfiguring all slurmctld
and slurmd daemons.
All slurmd daemons must know each node in the system to forward
messages in support of hierarchical communications.

It is advisable to establish baseline node configurations,
especially if the cluster is heterogeneous.

## MPI SUPPORT[#SECTION_MPI-SUPPORT](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
MPI use depends upon the type of MPI being used.
There are three fundamentally different modes of operation used
by these various MPI implementations.
1. Slurm directly launches the tasks and performs initialization
of communications through the PMI2 or PMIx APIs.
For example: "srun -n16 a.out".
2. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using Slurm's infrastructure (OpenMPI).
3. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using some mechanism other than Slurm,
such as SSH or RSH.
These tasks are initiated outside of Slurm's monitoring
or control. Slurm's epilog should be configured to purge
these tasks when the job's allocation is relinquished,
or the use of pam_slurm_adopt is highly recommended.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
Executing srun sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from srun or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run srun or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to srun to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

## MPI SUPPORT[#SECTION_MPI-SUPPORT](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
MPI use depends upon the type of MPI being used.
There are three fundamentally different modes of operation used
by these various MPI implementations.
1. Slurm directly launches the tasks and performs initialization
of communications through the PMI2 or PMIx APIs.
For example: "srun -n16 a.out".
2. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using Slurm's infrastructure (OpenMPI).
3. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using some mechanism other than Slurm,
such as SSH or RSH.
These tasks are initiated outside of Slurm's monitoring
or control. Slurm's epilog should be configured to purge
these tasks when the job's allocation is relinquished,
or the use of pam_slurm_adopt is highly recommended.

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
jobs that can run simultaneously on the node (i.e. cores).
The total count of shards available on a node should be configured in
the slurm.conf file (e.g. "NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2,shard:64").
Several options are available for configuring shards in the gres.conf file

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the
node is powered down). When the node is powered down, the those features
become available but not active. Any feature not defined by
NodeFeaturesPlugins are always active.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- A node feature is a label/attribute attached to a node (e.g., gpu_v100, ssd_local, nvlink, large_mem). Features are used by the scheduler to filter/choose which nodes are eligible for a job; requesting a feature restricts placement to nodes that expose that feature.
- Features can be static (defined in slurm.conf) or dynamic/changeable (managed by NodeFeaturesPlugins/helpers or set via scontrol). Dynamic features may be “available” but not yet “active” (common for cloud/power-save nodes) and activating a feature can require powering/rebooting a node — which affects placement latency.
- There are two related mechanisms:
  - --constraint (feature matching / node labels): pick nodes that list the requested feature(s).
  - --extra / extra_constraints (JSON numeric/boolean attributes + expression language, only when SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints): lets you ask for numeric comparisons and Boolean expressions (e.g. gpu_mem>=16 & foo=true) for finer selection.

How features affect placement (what you should expect)
- Eligibility: Any job that requests a feature is only eligible for nodes that advertise that feature. Fewer eligible nodes usually means longer queue times.
- Fragmentation & packing: Tight feature constraints reduce the pool the scheduler can pack on and may increase fragmentation (free resources that can’t satisfy constrained jobs).
- Backfill accuracy: If you use extra_constraints or frequently-changing features, Slurm’s backfill planner may be less accurate (the docs warn that changing node extra data often harms backfill planning).
- Dynamically-changeable features can delay allocation: if the controller must power/reboot a node (or call a helper) to activate a feature, the job may be delayed until that process completes.
- Power-save / cloud nodes: features defined by NodeFeaturesPlugins are available when nodes are powered down and become active only after the node is allocated and powered on. Requesting such features tells Slurm it may allocate and power-on those nodes to satisfy the job.
- Scheduling logic: features are filters (yes/no, or expression matches). They are not resources like CPUs or GPUs (TRES). Requesting a feature does not consume it — it only restricts placement to nodes that have it.
- Heterogeneous allocations: when nodes differ in features, the scheduler may create heterogeneous job allocations (different components with different features) if the job requests multiple component types or uses nodesets.

Common examples and usage
- Define features in slurm.conf (NodeName=... Feature=f1,f2) or set/update them with scontrol:
  - scontrol update NodeName=node123 Features=ssd_local,gpu_a100
- Request a feature at submit time:
  - sbatch --constraint=gpu_a100 myjob.sh
  - You can combine feature expressions (site behavior may vary — check your local docs/policy); for more complex numeric/boolean matching use --extra with extra_constraints enabled:
    - sbatch --extra 'gpu_mem>=16 & nvlink=true' myjob.sh
- Use nodesets to group feature-selected nodes in partition config (NodeSet ... Feature=...).

How to inspect features on your cluster
- scontrol show node <nodename> — shows Features= and Extra= fields for that node.
- sinfo and scontrol show config / helpers.conf for site-level feature/plugin configuration.
- If your site uses node feature helpers, look at helpers.conf and NodeFeaturesPlugins in slurm.conf to understand which features are dynamic and whether a helper/reboot is required.

Practical recommendations / best practices

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:

slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'

```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Node features are arbitrary labels (strings) attached to nodes that describe capabilities or configuration (examples: gpu, v100, ssd, ib, highmem). They let users request nodes with particular capabilities without changing partitions.
- Jobs request features with --constraint (or -C) using a boolean expression. The scheduler filters candidate nodes to those whose feature set satisfies the expression; only those nodes are considered for placement.

What a "feature" is and how it’s stored
- Declared in slurm.conf as Feature= on NodeName lines, or provided dynamically by a NodeFeatures plugin / helper.
- Features are just tags/strings (not counted resources). Some features may be “available but not active” (common for cloud/power-managed nodes); requesting such a feature can trigger the controller to activate/power-on the node at allocation time.
- Changing some features via helpers may require a node reboot.

How to request features (constraint expressions)
- Request with sbatch/srun/salloc: --constraint=<expr> (or -C <expr>).
- Expression grammar (common operators):
  - AND: & (or comma , in some docs) — both sides must match
  - OR: | — either side matches
  - NOT: ! — node must not have that feature
  - Parentheses () to group expressions
- Examples:
  - -C gpu        → node must have feature "gpu"
  - -C "gpu&v100" → node must have both gpu and v100
  - -C "gpu|tpu"  → node with gpu OR tpu
  - -C "!infiniband" → node without feature "infiniband"
  - -C "(v100|a100)&gpu" → gpu nodes with either v100 or a100 tags

How features affect placement and scheduling behavior
- Filtering: The constraint expression filters the set of candidate nodes before the scheduler considers resources on them. If no nodes satisfy the constraint, the job remains pending.
- Availability vs activation: If a feature is listed as available but inactive (cloud/power-managed), the controller may allocate and activate the node to satisfy the job. This can increase job startup latency.
- Backfill and fragmentation: Using many, narrow, or frequently-changing features reduces the pool of eligible nodes and can fragment resources, which may increase queueing time and reduce backfill effectiveness. The Slurm docs warn that frequent changes to node extra/feature data hurt backfill accuracy.
- Features are not resource counters: Two jobs can request the same feature; Slurm still enforces resource limits (CPUs, memory, gres) per node but does not limit feature usage unless combined with other controls.
- Partition scope: Constraints are applied within the chosen partition(s). Requesting a partition plus a constraint limits placement to nodes in that partition that match the constraint.
- Interaction with GRES: Hardware that has Slurm GRES (e.g., GPUs) should normally be requested via --gres=gpu:N. Some sites also tag GPU nodes with a feature (e.g., gpu or v100). Prefer --gres for counting and allocation semantics and use features for non-counted capabilities (special NICs, accelerators that aren’t configured as GRES, licensed software, local SSD).
- Extra constraints: Slurm also supports node "Extra" fields (SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints) with richer comparison operators; these are different from simple Feature tags and use a small expression language.

Practical tips / best practices
- Use short, stable, documented feature names (alphanumeric, no operator chars).
- Prefer --gres for devices you need counted (GPUs, MICs).
- Keep the number of distinct feature combinations small to avoid fragmentation.
- For cloud/power-managed nodes, be aware requests can power-on nodes and add latency — document that to users.
- To inspect node features on your cluster: sinfo or scontrol show node (e.g., sinfo -Nl or scontrol show node <nodename>) to see the Feature list.
- If you need complex node-selection logic (e.g., key/value metadata comparisons), look at SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints and Extra node fields.

If you want, I can:
- Show current node features on this cluster (sinfo / scontrol show node), or
- Suggest a constraint for a specific job profile you have (tell me what hardware or capability you need).

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Summary: node features are per-node labels (the Feature attribute) that the Slurm scheduler uses to filter which nodes are eligible for a job. Requesting features restricts placement to nodes that expose those features; features can be combined with logical operators and can be dynamic (requiring activation/reboot on some configurations), so they affect both which nodes are chosen and how long allocation may take.

What "features" are
- A Feature is a free-text attribute set on a Node (slurm.conf NodeName=... Feature=foo,bar or via helper plugins). Typical uses: indicate hardware types (a100, v100), interconnect/PCI config (nvlink), software stacks, or special site capabilities.
- They are simply node attributes — not resources like CPUs/GPU TRES — but are used by the scheduler to filter nodes.

How you request them
- Use --constraint (short -C) with sbatch/salloc/srun: e.g. sbatch -C v100 or sbatch -C "v100&nvlink".
- Boolean combinations supported: & (AND), | (OR), and parentheses for grouping. Examples:
  - -C "v100" (nodes with feature v100)
  - -C "v100&nvlink" (nodes with both features)
  - -C "v100|a100" (nodes with either)
  - -C "(v100&nvlink)|a100" (grouped logic)
- Quoting the constraint string is recommended to protect shell characters.

Dynamic/changeable features
- NodeFeaturesPlugins and helpers.conf can make some features changeable or “rebootable.” Such features may be inactive until a helper activates them; requesting them can trigger activation (which may reboot the node or cause a helper program to run) and therefore add delay.
- For cloud/power-save nodes, features can be “available but not active” when a node is powered down; allocation can power/activate them at allocation time.
- Any feature not managed by a node-features plugin is always active.

Scheduler behavior / placement consequences
- Feature filtering reduces eligible nodes. Narrow constraints can cause longer queue wait times or fragmentation (hard-to-fill allocations).
- If you request features that are inactive and require helper action or node reboot, the allocation will be delayed until activation completes (or the node is not used).
- Features do not imply exclusivity or resource reservation by themselves — they only select nodes. If you need exclusive use, use other sbatch options (e.g., --exclusive) or partition policies.
- Features interact with other selectors (partition, QOS, TRES, GRES). For GPU-specific selection it’s common to use GRES for GPU quantities and features to select a GPU model or interconnect.
- For multi-node jobs: all allocated nodes must satisfy the constraint unless you use advanced placement options; this can make large allocations harder to satisfy.

Operational notes & best practices
- Prefer stable, well-documented feature names (e.g., vendor_model or a100_80gb) to avoid confusion.
- Use partitions for large, permanent separations (e.g., all A100 nodes) and features for ad-hoc differences or orthogonal properties.
- Only make features changeable (requiring helper/reboot) when necessary; otherwise mark them as always active to avoid allocation delays.
- If you need richer matching (key/value, comparisons), Slurm supports extra-constraints / Extra fields (when enabled) which let you do key=value and comparison operators with boolean logic.
- To inspect node features on your cluster: use sinfo/scontrol show node (e.g., sinfo -N or scontrol show node nodename) to see the Feature list.

If you want, I can:
- Show current nodes and their Feature lists on this cluster (sinfo / scontrol show node), or
- Suggest feature names and a constraint expression for a concrete workload you have. Which would you like?

## Accounting Interpretation [#accounting-interpretation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html)
Slurm accounting is mainly focused on parallel computing. For this reason it
gathers statistics at a "task level". A task is a set of user processes which
run in a step, which is part of a job. A user can submit a step with many
parallel tasks, e.g. by calling `srun -n`.
The [JobAcctGather](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) plugin
gathers metrics for some [Trackable Resources (TRES)](https://slurm.schedmd.com/tres.html),
like cpu, memory, energy, etc., at a given interval in the [JobAcctGatherFrequency](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
defined in slurm.conf, or by using the `--acct-freq` option in the
command line. A poll of data is also triggered at the start or the end of a
step.

## Command Options[#command](https://slurm.schedmd.com/core_spec.html)
All job allocation commands ( salloc , sbatch and srun )
accept the -S or --core-spec option with a core count value
argument (e.g. "-S 1" or "--core-spec=2").
The count identifies the number of cores to be reserved for system overhead on
each allocated compute node. Note that the --core-spec option will be
ignored if AllowSpecResourcesUsage is not enabled in your slurm.conf.
Each job's core specialization count can be viewed using the scontrol ,
sview or squeue command.
Specification of a core specialization count for a job step is ignored
(i.e. for the srun command within a job allocation created using the
salloc or sbatch command).
Use the squeue command with the "%X" format option to see the count
(it is not reported in the default output format).
The scontrol and sview commands can also be used to modify
